body:
## Module 2 in two minutes

**A baseline taken after you switch something on is not a baseline.** It is a measurement of the new state, and there is no recovery: every other mistake in this track is fixable later, this one isn't.

A baseline is a named query, against a stated population, on a stated date, saved somewhere you'll find it. Not a memory. Memories reshape themselves around outcomes: after a deployment everyone remembers the before as worse than it was, uniformly and sincerely.

**Four numbers, under an hour, before anything is enabled.** Volume. Cycle time, with *time to first response* separated out, because those two move independently and conflating them hides the interesting result. **The repeat rate**, which is the number that detects a wrong answer and which almost nobody captures. And the top five categories by count, because if a deployment changes the *mix* rather than the volume, that's the most important thing that happened.

Save the query, not just the answer. And write down the population — otherwise the comparison six months later quietly uses a denominator that flatters the result.

And note the asymmetry: when the talent team says they can't measure their AI, that's often true. **You own the ticket system, the logs, the transaction volumes and the cycle times. When you say it, it means you did not.**

### +19 to −35

IBM's AskHR launched in 2017 and almost nobody used it. So in 2018 the company required it: more than 20,000 employees told to use the assistant rather than contact HR directly. Usage went to essentially everyone. On an adoption dashboard that year is a triumph.

**HR's satisfaction score went from +19 to −35 within the first year.**

The only reason anyone knows is that IBM was already measuring satisfaction *before* the mandate, on a metric about experience rather than usage. With adoption metrics alone (which is what almost every deployment reports) that year is indistinguishable from success: usage up, tickets down, cost per interaction down.

They rebuilt around what employees actually wanted and satisfaction recovered into the +80s. Today IBM reports AskHR settling ~94% of routine requests. **Both facts are the same company's, and the success figures are unaudited self-report**. We hold a number that flatters our argument to the standard we hold IBM's unverifiable attrition claim. The −35 is the one this module leans on, because self-reporting a failure is the more credible direction.

**So: activity metrics survive bad deployments, and they also survive mandates.** The indicator that doesn't: **do people come back when they have a choice?**

**The full module adds two things.** First, where the rework goes: a deployment you run relocates it onto employees, managers and coordinators, none of which appears in your project's numbers, and all of which appears in **your queue.** Tag AI-involved contacts and repeat contacts from the day before go-live, and you become the rework detector for the whole function's AI. That is an advantage and a political problem; Module 8 handles the second part.

Second, why scope decides everything. Two randomized coaching trials four years apart reached opposite conclusions with the same class of technology: the narrow, structured one worked, the open-ended one showed no benefit, and one researcher co-authored both. So: **narrow the scope until it works, rather than widening it until it fails.** A scope wide enough to be impressive is usually wide enough that no result could disconfirm it.

Then the artifact. **A deployment without a written condition under which you'd turn it off is not a pilot, it's an installation.** Four parts: a computable threshold, a date, a named person, and **a rollback somebody has actually performed** — an untested rollback is a hope. The test for whether yours is real: *could it fire while the sponsor still wants the project?* If not, you've written a review date with a number attached.
